title: The Abused and the Silence
subtitle: When the church protected its own name and left the wounded to carry the shame that was never theirs.
question: What does God require of a people who learned to keep the abuser comfortable and the abused quiet?
whyItMatters:
There is a particular grief that has no language for itself. It belongs to the person who was harmed inside the one place that promised to be safe, and then watched the room close around the one who harmed them. The hand on the shoulder went to the wrong shoulder. The benefit of the doubt was spent on the wrong person. This is not a footnote to the life of the church. For thousands of people it is the whole memory of the church, and they carry it into every Sunday they cannot bring themselves to attend.

If you are reading this and you were one of them, hear one thing before anything else. What happened to you was not the cost of belonging, and it was not yours to absorb so the institution could go on undisturbed. The silence that followed your wound was a second wound, and Scripture treats it as such. We write this slowly, because the subject deserves slowness, and because too much of what the church has said about abuse has been said in a hurry to move past it.
biblicalFoundation:
Jesus, who was gentle with almost everyone, became terrible on one subject. He said it would be better for a person to have a millstone hung around the neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble. He did not soften it. He did not add a clause about reputations or the good a person had otherwise done. The severity is the point. The God who is slow to anger has a place where his patience ends, and it ends here, at the harm done to the small and the trusting.

The Bible does not hide what was done to Tamar in 2 Samuel 13. It records the abuse, and then it records something almost worse. Her brother told her to be quiet, to keep the matter to herself, because the man who harmed her was a son of the king. David, the man after God's own heart, was angry and did nothing. So a daughter lived desolate in her brother's house while the household calculated what the truth would cost the family. The text does not approve of this. It simply lets us see it, the way it always lets us see the failures of the men it will not flatter. The cover-up is older than the church, and Scripture names it as sin even when no one in the story will.

Through Ezekiel the Lord turned on the shepherds who fed themselves and let the flock scatter, who ruled with force and harshness and did not strengthen the weak or bind up the injured or seek the lost. Woe to the shepherds, he said, and then he said something the institution should never be able to forget. I will rescue my flock from their mouths. The God of Ezekiel 34 does not see the shepherd and the sheep as equals when one has devoured the other. He takes the side of the devoured. He always has.

And he hears. The cry of the oppressed reaches him, as the blood of Abel reached him from the ground, as the cry of Israel reached him from under the whip. Paul tells the church to have nothing to do with the works of darkness, but instead to expose them, because what is done in secret is shameful even to mention. The instinct of the gospel is not to cover. It is to bring into the light. The repeated command of the law, woven through prophet and psalm, is justice for the widow and the orphan, for the ones with no power to demand it. A church that protects the powerful against the powerless has not made a small mistake about procedure. It has stood on the wrong side of the God who wrote that law.
keyTexts: Matthew 18:6 to 7 (the millstone and the warning against causing little ones to stumble)
2 Samuel 13:1 to 22 (the abuse of Tamar and the silence of the house of David)
Ezekiel 34:1 to 16 (woe to the shepherds who scatter the flock and do not protect it)
Exodus 22:22 to 24 (the cry of the widow and the orphan that God himself will hear)
Ephesians 5:11 to 13 (expose the works of darkness rather than cover them)
Psalm 10:17 to 18 (the Lord hears the desire of the afflicted and does justice for the oppressed)

churchRecord.led: At its best the church has believed the one whose word cost them everything to give, has put the safety of the vulnerable above the comfort of the powerful, and has been the place where a survivor was met not with a strategy but with a presence that did not flinch. It has built the orphanage and the shelter, sat with the abused through the long aftermath, and reported the crime to the authorities the moment it learned of it, accepting whatever that truth would cost the institution. This is the church doing what its Lord did.
churchRecord.failed: And it has done the opposite, on a scale that should leave us unable to speak quickly about anything. It has moved the abuser quietly to another parish, another church plant, another mission field, and called it grace. It has asked the abused to forgive before they were safe and to be reconciled before there was repentance. It has feared the lawsuit more than the sin and the scandal more than the wound. It has made the survivor the problem, because the survivor's truth was inconvenient to the institution's name. We did this. Not a rogue few in the corner of the church, but the church, the body to which we belong, and we will not understand it until we stop calling it their failure and start calling it ours.

whereWeAgree: Across every wing of the church there is at least the stated conviction that a child or a vulnerable adult must be protected before any reputation, that the institution's name is worth less than a single person made in the image of God, and that the cry of the abused must reach someone who will act.
captureLeft: The left can turn the protection of the vulnerable into a posture of permanent suspicion, where accusation alone is treated as conviction and the careful work of establishing the truth is mistaken for betrayal of the wounded. In its worst form it cares more about being seen on the right side than about the slow, costly labor of actually protecting anyone.
captureRight: The right can treat the institution and its leaders as nearly sacred, so that a man's standing, his fruitfulness, his doctrine, become reasons to doubt the one he harmed. In its worst form it dresses the cover-up in the language of grace and restoration, and asks the abused to absorb the cost so the ministry can go on.
whereWeDiffer: We will differ, honestly and sometimes sharply, on what fair process looks like, on how to weigh an accusation before it is established, and on how to hold the protection of the vulnerable together with due care for the accused. That disagreement is real and worth having. It is not a license to do nothing, and it has too often been used as one.
theCost: To stand here costs the church the thing it has most wanted to keep, which is its reputation. It means reporting to the authorities instead of handling it within. It means believing the costly word over the convenient one, opening the records, naming the names, and letting the truth do its damage to the institution we love. It means the powerful man in the room loses, and we lose with him, because we chose the small and the wounded over our own good name. There is no version of this that does not cost us. That is how we will know we have finally told the truth.
charge: If you have been abused inside the church, you do not owe the institution your silence, and you never did. The God of Ezekiel takes your side. If you covered for an abuser to protect a name, the millstone passage is not about someone else. Tell the truth now, to the people who can act on it, and let it cost what it costs. And to the rest of us who watched and said nothing, the charge is the same. Open the door. Believe the wounded. Let the light in where we have spent so long keeping it out.
